extracted.intended_audience: immigration attorneys, advocates, DHS officers, regulated public, and policy stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and procedural guidance for how DHS officers should evaluate whether an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge when applying for admission or adjustment of status, including factors to consider, exemptions, bond rules, and the economic cost-benefit framing of the proposed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of current and/or past receipt of means-tested public benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS may consider any current and/or past receipt of means-tested public benefits by aliens when making a public charge inadmissibility determination if the alien seeks adjustment of status in a category that is not exempt from the public charge ground of inadmissibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is described as reasonable and aligned with the statute; consistent with IIRIRA and PRWORA. DHS proposes to remove regulatory limits that would have limited consideration to only certain benefit types (e.g., public cash assistance and long-term institutionalization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of regulation excluding benefits available to refugees (8 CFR 212.22(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to remove the provision that would not consider any public benefits received by certain aliens eligible for refugee-type supports when making a public charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS's rationale: aliens previously granted refugee-available benefits are not different from other aliens; Congress simultaneously made some aliens eligible for benefits while making them subject to the public charge ground. Officers would take into account time-limited eligibility where applicable (e.g., expired grants to Afghan nationals and Ukrainians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory minimum factors for public charge determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consular and DHS officers must, at a minimum, consider the alien's age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills. DHS may also consider any affidavit of support submitted under section 213A of the INA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS will continue to collect this information through Form I-485 and Form I-693 and will consider these minimum factors while also allowing officers to consider additional evidence on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances / individualized, fact-specific determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Officers should make highly individualized, fact-specific, case-by-case public charge inadmissibility decisions based on the totality of each alien's individual circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed rule removes rigid regulatory definitions and standards (from the 2022 Final Rule) to enable officers to consider other evidence in DHS records or systems that bears on likelihood of becoming a public charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions and waivers (statutory) vs. removing regulatory list (8 CFR 212.23)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain categories of aliens are exempt from the public charge ground under statute (e.g., refugees/asylees under INA sec. 209(c), Cuban Adjustment Act classes) and statutory waivers exist; DHS proposes to remove the duplicative regulatory list of exemptions and waivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes the list is redundant with the USCIS Policy Manual and Form I-485 (Part 9, Item 56); Policy Manual and forms can be updated more readily than regulations, reducing risk of regulatory text falling out of date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability statement removal (8 CFR 212.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to remove 8 CFR 212.20, a section that introduced the following sections and stated applicability to applicants for admission or adjustment unless exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because DHS proposes to remove 212.21–212.23, 212.20 would serve no purpose; the public charge ground still applies to applicants unless exempt by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public charge bond breach and cancellation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS proposes to amend public charge bond provisions to state that receipt of any means-tested public benefit during the effective period of the bond, or otherwise being noncompliant with bond conditions, will result in breach of the public charge bond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS also proposes to remove the ground for cancellation allowing DHS to cancel a public charge bond at any time if it determines 'that the alien is not likely at any time to become a public charge' as practically infeasible, and to restructure cancellation and breach provisions for clarity (8 CFR 103.6(c) revisions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of time-limited benefit eligibility as a forward-looking factor
rubrics_metrics.description: When eligibility for public benefits is time-limited (e.g., initial grants to certain Afghans and Ukrainians that have expired), USCIS officers would take time-limited eligibility into account when making forward-looking public charge determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes many of these grants have expired and many aliens have obtained other status or have pending applications; officers should factor this into the totality analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit of Support requirement and its legal effect (INA section 213A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain family-based and some employment-based immigrants are required to submit a sufficient Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA; failure to meet this requirement results in inadmissibility under the public charge ground without review of the statutory minimum factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a sponsor executes the affidavit, it establishes a legally enforceable contract obligating the sponsor to financially support the applicant and to reimburse benefit-granting agencies if covered benefits are received during the enforceability period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data/population estimation methodology for economic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS estimates the affected population using historical Form I-485 filing data and approvals, using a 6-year average (FY2019–FY2024) to estimate annual totals and then removing those classes exempt from public charge review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS uses these population estimates to project the annual average number of aliens filing I-485 (projected 727,192) and the subset subject to public charge review (projected 587,706). Tables (VI.3–VI.7) detail receipts, approvals, and denials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic requirements under Executive Orders and OMB guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must assess costs and benefits of regulatory alternatives, quantify costs and benefits where possible, reduce costs, harmonize rules, and promote flexibility (E.O. 12866, 13563, 14192), and prepare accounting statements as required by OMB Circular A-4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposed rule is designated a 'significant regulatory action' and reviewed by OMB. E.O. 14192 includes requirements to offset incremental costs by eliminating costs of prior regulations where applicable, but this rule is not an E.O. 14192 regulatory action for immigration functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipated effects on transfer payments and indirect economic impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS anticipates reductions in Federal and State transfer payments due to disenrollment or forgone enrollment in public benefits by members of households that include aliens, and recognizes downstream impacts on healthcare providers, retailers, producers, landlords, and local economies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS estimates potential reductions (e.g., approx. $8.97 billion annually; 10-year discounted reductions of ~$76.48B at 3% and ~$62.97B at 7%), but notes these are approximations influenced by external factors and limited data; methodology draws on prior rule assumptions and disenrollment rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disenrollment/forgone enrollment rate methodology (transfer estimates)
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS uses a disenrollment/forgone enrollment rate (2.5% in 2019 Final Rule; 3.1% in 2022 Final Rule) applied to estimated populations of public benefits recipients in households including aliens to estimate reductions in transfer payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS estimated these rates by dividing annual number of approved aliens who adjusted status by the estimated alien population; recognizes uncertainty and that external policies (e.g., changes to Medicaid/SNAP) affect enrollment and estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of other evidence in DHS records/systems
rubrics_metrics.description: By removing the 2022 Final Rule's limited enumerated factor list, DHS intends officers to consider other evidence contained in DHS records or systems that bears on whether an alien is likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows a broader evidentiary base beyond only past/current receipt of specified benefit types and the statutory minimum factors; DHS plans to provide interpretive and policy tools to guide determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of CBP and port-of-entry adjudications (scope/limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The economic analysis focuses on applicants for adjustment of status using Form I-485 and does not quantify impacts for aliens seeking admission at ports of entry, though CBP is generally subject to the public charge ground and may incur costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS qualitatively acknowledges potential CBP impacts but cannot quantify them due to data limitations; CBP activities (examining noncitizens at ports) are noted but excluded from population estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance interests and transitional interpretive/policy tools
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS acknowledges the regulated public may have relied on aspects of the 2022 Final Rule and requests comments on what parts engendered reliance and how to address those reliance interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS indicates it will explain how officers would conduct determinations if the rescission is finalized, reference controlling precedent and case law, and plans to provide interpretive and policy tools to balance self-sufficiency, fortify officer discretion, and support accuracy, consistency, and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity of denial on public charge grounds historically and role of Form I-864 insufficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical data show adjustment-of-status denials on public charge grounds are rare; many denials under prior rules were due to missing or insufficient Form I-864 rather than totality-of-circumstances analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS presents denial counts (e.g., average denials on public charge grounds were a small fraction of I-485 denials) to contextualize expected impacts; emphasizes statutory affidavit requirement's central role where applicable.
